text: One of Jost Amman's pupils said the drawings he made in four years would have filled a hay wagon. About 1,500 prints are attributed to him, and many of his original drawings are in the Berlin print room. He was the son of a professor of Classics and Logic in Zürich and moved to Nuremberg in 1560, where he worked first with Virgil Solis. He was one of the last major producers of woodcuts for books, as engravings were gradually taking over that role. Like most woodcut artists, he normally let a specialist cut the block. He died in 1591.

Jean Mariette came from a line of wealthy print publishers, his father Pierre II and his grandfather Pierre I. He studied drawing, painting and engraving with his brother-in-law Jean-Baptiste Corneille, but he stopped painting after Charles Le Brun saw some of his engravings and advised him to focus on that. After his father's death he took over one of the family businesses on the rue Saint-Jacques. Over his career he published almost 900 prints. He was the father of Pierre-Jean Mariette and died in 1742.

William Callow was apprenticed to Copley Fielding, who taught him plein air sketching, and he went on to study under Theodore and Thales Fielding, where he learned to colour prints and make aquatints. In 1829 Thales found him work as an engraver in Paris, alongside his friend Charles Bentley. After he showed a watercolour of Richmond Hill at the Paris Salon of 1831, he was offered a job teaching the family of King Louis Philippe. For several years he gave lessons to the Duc de Nemours and Princess Clémentine. He died in 1908.

Wojciech Weiss gave up music training to study art at the Academy of Fine Arts in Kraków under Leon Wyczółkowski. His family was Polish and in exile in Bukovina. He first painted historical or mythological subjects, then switched to Expressionism after Stanisław Przybyszewski deeply influenced him. He later joined the Vienna Secession, and he was one of the first Polish Art Nouveau poster designers. Near the end of his life he contributed to Socialist realist painting in Poland. His Self-Portrait with Masks dates from 1900.

Alfred Zoff began by studying medicine, though he had decided early to become an artist, and in 1869 he took classes in Graz with the landscape painter Hermann von Königsbrunn. After his father died, his mother moved to Klagenfurt, and he often visited to paint. It remained a favorite place for the rest of his life. He finished his studies in 1890 at Karlsruhe with Gustav Schönleber, who acquainted him with the Barbizon school. From 1907 he was a professor of landscape and still-life painting at the academy in Graz.

After a disagreement about his art studies, George Hayter ran away to sea in 1808 as a midshipman in the Royal Navy. His father, a miniature painter, got him released, and they agreed that George would assist him while pursuing his own studies. In 1809 he secretly married Sarah Milton, a lodger at his father's house. He specialised in portraits and in large works with several hundred individual portraits. Queen Victoria appointed him her Principal Painter in Ordinary and knighted him in 1841.

Until he was twenty, Constant Troyon labored at the minute details of porcelain ornament, because his father was connected with the porcelain manufactory at Sèvres. By twenty-one he was travelling the country painting landscapes for as long as his money lasted. When it ran out, he went back to work as a decorator with the first china manufacturer he met. Only late in life did he find his subject in animals, and then he gained international recognition. He belonged to the Barbizon school and died in 1865.

Henri Lebasque started at the art school in Angers and moved to Paris in 1886, where he studied under Léon Bonnat. He helped Ferdinand Humbert with the murals at the Panthéon and met Camille Pissarro and Auguste Renoir. Contact with Vuillard and Bonnard coloured his vision. From Seurat and Signac he learned a colour theory that used complementary colours in shading. In 1903 he was a founding member of the Salon d'Automne with his friend Henri Matisse. His work hangs in museums in Angers, Lille and Paris.

Hanns Lautensack is sometimes wrongly called Hans Sebald Lautensack. His father Paul was a painter in Bamberg, but the family settled in Nuremberg when he was a child, and he lived there for most of his life. In 1556 he was working in Vienna, perhaps summoned by Emperor Ferdinand I to make pictures of his collection of ancient coins. His etchings carry the monogram H. S. L. They fall into two periods, the Nuremberg years and the Vienna years. His brother Heinrich was a goldsmith.

Adam Perelle learned from his father Gabriel Pérelle and then worked as his assistant. Like his brother Nicolas, he made copperplate engravings of landscapes and monuments. He became engraver of the King and taught drawing and painting in high society, and Louis III, Prince of Condé, was one of his pupils. In 1667 he signed a contract with Erik Dahlbergh. For two Swedish books he made 13 plates of battles and 32 images of landscapes and buildings. He died in 1695.

At twelve Matthijs Maris registered at the Hague Academy of Art but did not pass the entrance exam, so he took lessons from the academy's secretary and was admitted a year later. Queen Sophie's grant helped him follow his brother Jacob to Antwerp, where they rented rooms together. Later the brothers painted in Oosterbeek with Gerard Bilders and Anton Mauve. He began in the Hague School, like his brothers Jacob and Willem, but his later works moved toward a unique style influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites. He died in 1917.

Koloman Moser designed a wide array of things, from postage stamps and magazine vignettes to fashion, stained glass, porcelain, tableware, silver, jewellery and furniture. He was the oldest of three siblings, and he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts and the School of Applied Arts in Vienna, where he also taught from 1899. He drew on the clean lines and repetitive motifs of classical Greek and Roman art, in reaction to the Baroque decadence around him. He was a leading artist of the Vienna Secession and a co-founder of the Wiener Werkstätte. He died in 1918.

Robert Hills studied first under John Alexander Gresse and then enrolled at the Royal Academy of Arts. He mostly painted rural scenes, particularly farm animals. He was also known for drawing animals into the works of other artists, such as George Barret Jr. and George Fennell Robson. His Sketches in Flanders and Holland, with aquatints by himself, was published in 1816. Some of his works are in the British Museum. He lived from 1769 to 1844 and was born in Islington.

Johan Christian Dahl taught Thomas Fearnley, who became a leading representative of Norwegian romantic nationalism in painting. He came from Frederikshald, now Halden, the son of a merchant whose own father had moved from Yorkshire to Norway. His brother Carl Frederik was an astronomer and professor. He married Cecilia Andresen, daughter of his benefactor, the banker Nicolai Andresen. In the autumn of 1841 the couple went to Amsterdam for the birth of their only child. Fearnley died in 1842.

Miklós Barabás painted from an early age and was a pupil of Johann Ender in Vienna for a while. Back in Kolozsvár he learned lithography from Gábor Barra. In Italy he learned watercolour from the Scot William Leighton Leitch, six years older, and the two became friends and toured the Lago Maggiore region together. Leitch influenced his later work. Barabás is mostly known for portraits, among them one of the young Franz Liszt. He settled in Pest in 1855.

Henry Taunt worked first for his father, who was a plumber, but he decided he did not want that trade. From the age of eleven he worked for a tailor, then a stationer, then a bookshop and auction room, all on the High Street in Oxford. At fourteen he joined Edward Bracher, Oxford's first commercial photographer, who for some years had a monopoly in the city. Bracher promoted him from general assistant, and in 1858 Taunt took his first photographs for him. He died in 1922.

According to the RKD, Coenraet Decker was a pupil of Romeyn de Hooghe, and he married Aechje Jans in Sloterdijk when he was 23. He was a Dutch Golden Age engraver from Amsterdam. In the 1670s he worked on the map of Delft, a contract that he won together with Dirk van Bleiswijk for Bleiswijk's Description of Delft. He lived from 1650 to 1685.

Étienne Dupérac arrived in Rome in 1550 and became a skilled designer and engraver there. He is best known for his studies of Rome and its ruins. He published a bird's-eye view of ancient Rome with the buildings reconstructed, one of modern Rome, and a book of forty engravings of Roman monuments, I vestigi dell'antichità di Roma. A book of drawings of Roman ruins set beside reconstructions has been attributed to him, though his authorship has been questioned. He was also an architect, painter and garden designer. He died in 1604.

Jean Audran learned the rudiments of engraving from his father Germain and was then placed with his uncle Gérard Audran in Paris. He showed ability before he was twenty. In 1706 he was made engraver to the king, with a pension and apartments at the Gobelins. His prints include portraits of Louis XV after Gobert, the Duke d'Antin after Rigaud and Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni after Trevisani. He was the brother of Benoit Audran. He was born in Lyons and died in 1756.

Zacharias Dolendo was the brother of Bartholomeus Dolendo, whom he surpassed in style and correctness. He came from Leiden and is said to have been a disciple of Jacob de Gheyn. Some portraits by him are as neat as those by Wierix, and his plates are frequently marked with a cipher. He engraved William, Prince of Orange, in armour, Andromeda chained to the rock after his own design, and a set of small plates of the gods and goddesses copied from larger ones by Goltzius. He lived from 1561 to 1601.

Howard Russell Butler studied science and law before he became a painter. His early training came from William Shannon, and he visited the studio of his uncle William Stanley Haseltine. At Princeton he took a science degree in 1876, stayed on as an assistant professor of physics and rowed on the team. Later he persuaded Andrew Carnegie to fund Carnegie Lake near Princeton, and he painted a solar eclipse for the U.S. Naval Observatory. He also founded the American Fine Arts Society. He died in 1934.

Jean-Pierre Norblin de La Gourdaine started his career in France, but from 1774 to 1796 he lived in Poland, where several of the country's most notable families gave him commissions. His style showed the influence of Watteau and combined the Rococo tradition of fêtes galantes with a panorama of daily life and current political events, captured with journalistic accuracy. He made a gallery of portraits of all social classes in the last years of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Later he became influenced by Rembrandt as well. He died in 1830.

Ludwig Richter was the son of an engraver in Dresden and received his training from him. As a painter he aimed at a thorough blending of the figure with the landscape, as in Ferry at the Schreckenstein. He produced several woodcuts for the Grimm fairy tales, and his work is described as typically German and homely. Erhard and Chodowiecki influenced him strongly, and he stood for both Romanticism and Biedermeier. One of his protégés was Hermann Lungkwitz. He died in 1884.

Willem Claesz. Heda painted only still lifes. He was the son of the Haarlem city architect Claes Pietersz, and his uncle was the painter Cornelis Claesz Heda. Almost nothing is known of his early life, since no surviving pieces are dated to that period, and his earliest known work is a Vanitas. He is known for his innovation of the late breakfast genre of still life, with monochromatic colour and skillful texturing. He died around 1680.

Jan Fyt was the son of a wealthy merchant from Sint-Niklaas who lived in Antwerp. In 1621 he was registered at the Antwerp Guild of St Luke as an apprentice of Hans van den Berghe, who had trained with Goltzius in Haarlem and later with Rubens. He then likely finished his training with the animal painter Frans Snyders. He painted still lifes and animals, and he also combined them, for example game, flowers and fish under a festoon of flowers. He was probably the master of Pieter Boel, who worked in a very similar style.

Dancker Danckerts belonged to a large Amsterdam family of engravers, cartographers, print-sellers and publishers, and his parents were Cornelis Danckerts and Anne Minne of Leiden. He was known for etchings of paintings and maps and for his publications. His works are collected in museums, libraries and archives around the world. He was active in Amsterdam from 1654 to 1666, with a probable trip to Venice in 1656, according to the inscription on a drawing in Parma.

Nils Kreuger's father ran a lumber and wood products business. Illness forced him to leave the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts, and later he studied at Edvard Perséus's private painting school. In 1881 he went to Paris and studied with Jean-Paul Laurens, and he spent much of his time painting outdoors in Grez-sur-Loing. He liked painting at dawn or dusk, in haze or rain. After 1885 he supported the Opponenterna, a group against the outmoded teaching at the Royal Academy, and helped create the Artists' Union. He died in 1930.

Cândido de Faria's father was a physician who specialised in cholera, founded the Hospital de Caridade de Laranjeiras and died in a cholera epidemic. The family moved to Rio de Janeiro, where the boy studied at the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios. He became a caricaturist, painter, lithographer and poster designer, and he emigrated to France in 1882. In France he designed posters for café-chantant performers and the cinema, and also for music scores. After he died in Paris in 1911, his workshop kept going and signed its work Atelier Faria.

Jean Mignon was active from 1537 to the mid-1550s and was one of the first group of artists in France to use etching for prints. He took part in the burst of activity at Fontainebleau in the 1540s. At least half of his prints, over thirty, use compositions by the Italian painter Luca Penni, and others use designs by Primaticcio. In all he made around sixty prints. Nothing is known about his origins or early life. His first appearance in documents is in the royal accounts of 1537, as a painter at the Palace of Fontainebleau.

Kristian Zahrtmann was known especially for history paintings of strong, tragic, legendary women in Danish history. He also painted landscapes, street scenes, folk scenes and portraits. With Peder Severin Krøyer and Theodor Esbern Philipsen he broke away from academicism and from the heritage of the Golden Age of Danish painting, in favor of naturalism and realism. He taught for many years and supported his students' individual styles, which affected the development of Danish art. His bold use of colour dazzled his contemporaries. He was born in Rønne on Bornholm and died in 1917.

Hans Vredeman de Vries is known for his books of ornament and of perspective, the latter from 1604. Born in Leeuwarden, he moved to Mechelen, where he designed ornaments for parades for Charles V and Philip II. He studied Vitruvius and Serlio, in translations by his teacher Pieter Coecke van Aelst, and became an internationally known specialist in perspective. In Antwerp he was appointed city architect and fortification engineer. After 1585 he had to flee the city because of the Spanish occupation, since he was a Protestant. He died in 1607.

Pieter van Bloemen became a master of the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in 1674, at the age of 17. He was a pupil of Simon Johannes van Douw, by some accounts from the age of 10. Two younger brothers were painters too. He travelled to Rome via Turin with one of them, and in 1688 they were registered in the parish of Sant'Andrea delle Fratte. He painted Italian landscapes with figures, equestrian battles, animals and market scenes. He died in 1720.

Jan Hendrik Weissenbruch came from an artistic family. His father Johannes ran a restaurant, painted in his free time and collected art, including works by Andreas Schelfhout. A cousin, Jan, was a well-known painter of townscapes, and another cousin was a lithographer, while his brother, uncle and nephew were all engravers. At sixteen he took drawing lessons. He was noted especially for his watercolours. He was born in The Hague in 1824 and died there in 1903.

Nothing is known about the education of Anton Ziegler, who was born in Vienna in 1793. He began writing at an early age, and several of his works went through repeated editions. He worked with artists such as Peter Johann Nepomuk Geiger. During the Revolutions of 1848 he served in the Vienna National Guard in the Wieden district. That April he published the first issue of a popular journal, Das große freie Oesterreich, with himself as editor-in-chief, but it died out after the fourth issue. He died in 1869.

Jan van Scorel's trip to Italy coincided with the brief reign of the only Dutch pope, Adrian VI, who made him a court painter and superintendent of his collection of antiquities. His stay in Italy lasted six years, and he also visited Nuremberg, Venice and Jerusalem. Venetian art had an important impact on his style. Unlike most Romanists he was a native of the northern Netherlands, where he stayed for most of his life. In 1530 he settled permanently in Utrecht and set up a large workshop on the Italian model. He died in 1562.

Antonio Zeno Shindler studied art in Paris and then moved to the United States with the anthropologist William Henry Blackmore. He worked as a professor at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia and later moved to Washington, D.C., where he worked for the Smithsonian American Art Museum. In 1867 Blackmore loaned him his photograph collection, and some of it went into the Smithsonian's first photograph exhibit. Shindler died in Washington in 1899 after falling off a streetcar.

For a few years from 1759 Hermanus Numan worked with his father in a lacquerware factory in Groningen. Then he apprenticed with Jan Augustini and worked in Haarlem with Egbert van Drielst, producing decorative wallpaper. Back in Groningen he worked for a while as a portraitist, and in 1768 he went to Paris to study engraving. He settled in Amsterdam and later joined the Felix Meritis artist community. His subjects were mostly landscapes, genre art and portraits, and he also made copies of paintings in Amsterdam collections. He died in 1820.

Antoine Masson learned engraving as an armorer's apprentice and had no other teaching. He came from Loury, near Orléans, and engraved 68 plates, mostly portraits. His best known subject is The Pilgrims of Emmaus, after Titian, nicknamed The Tablecloth because of the extreme care he took over the texture of the linen. His portrait of Guy Patin shows a mannerism, a nose formed from one spiral cut. The Académie Royale received him in 1679. He died in Paris in 1700.

Odoardo Fialetti first apprenticed in Bologna with Giovanni Battista Cremonini, and after travelling to Rome he moved to Venice to work in the studio of the elderly Tintoretto. He is listed as a member of the Venetian painters' guild from 1604 to 1612. In Venice he painted a St Agnes for the church of San Nicolò da Tolentino and scenes from the Life of St Dominic for the sacristy of Santi Giovanni e Paolo. His style became much looser and more dynamic in later life. He died in Venice.

Othon Friesz came from a long line of shipbuilders and sea captains in Le Havre. At school there he met his lifelong friend Raoul Dufy, and they studied at the Le Havre School of Fine Arts and then went to Paris together. In Paris he met Henri Matisse, Albert Marquet and Georges Rouault, and like them he rebelled against the academic teaching of Bonnat. He exhibited with the Fauves in 1907. The following year he went back to Normandy and to a much more traditional style, since his goals were firmly rooted in the past.

Ford Madox Brown spent the last years of his life painting the twelve Manchester Murals, which show the history of Manchester, for Manchester Town Hall. His grandfather was the medical theorist John Brown, and his father served as a purser in the Royal Navy. The family had little money and moved to Calais to find cheaper lodgings. Brown painted moral and historical subjects in a graphic, often Hogarthian version of the Pre-Raphaelite style. His painting Work took from 1852 to 1865. He died in 1893.

Deaf from birth, Albert Newsam lost his father, who drowned, when he was small, and a local hotel owner in Steubenville, Ohio, took him in. He showed talent early with chalk and pencil sketches. He was brought to Philadelphia and studied at the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf. He was an early practitioner of lithography in the United States, and he contributed many images to medical and sheet music books. His portraits of politicians, doctors, lawyers and businessmen raised the standing of lithography there. He died in 1864.

Benedito Calixto painted Brazil: its people and culture, from a portrait of the bandeirante Domingos Jorge Velho to the Proclamation of the Brazilian Republic, and scenes of the São Paulo coastline. His painting of the sinking of the SS Sirio is one of them. Unlike many artists of his time, he had a patron other than the state, an individual, and that was described as the most dependable source of patronage. He painted the Proclamation in 1893. He died in 1927.

Francesco Hayez was the youngest of five sons in a poor Venetian family, and his father was a fisherman of French origin. He showed a talent for drawing as a child, and at a very early age he was placed in the studio of his uncle Giovanni Binasco, an antiquarian who hoped to train him as a restorer of paintings. In 1798 he began to study painting under Francesco Maggiotto and had his first experience of the Neoclassical style. In mid-19th-century Milan he was known for grand historical paintings, political allegories and portraits. He died in 1882.

According to Vasari, Paris Bordone apprenticed briefly and unhappily with Titian, yet he kept a strand of Mannerist complexity and provincial vigor. He came from Treviso and had moved to Venice by late adolescence. His works of the 1520s include a Holy Family in Florence and a Sacra Conversazione with Donor in Glasgow. In 1525 he painted an altarpiece for the church of S. Agostino in Crema, a Madonna with St. Christopher and St George, which is now in the Palazzo Tadini collection at Lovere. He died in 1571.

Giovanni Fattori's family planned a career in commerce for him, but his skill at drawing persuaded them to apprentice him in 1845 to a local painter of religious themes, Giuseppe Baldini. The next year he moved to Florence, where he studied under Giuseppe Bezzuoli and at the Academy of Fine Arts. He began with historical themes and military subjects. In his middle years, inspired by the Barbizon school, he took to painting outdoors, with landscapes, rural scenes and scenes of military life. He belonged to the Macchiaioli. After 1884 he gave much energy to etching.

Gaetano Gandolfi grew up on an estate in the Po Valley near Bologna, which his father managed for a landowner. He followed his older brother Ubaldo to the Accademia Clementina in Bologna, where he won several prizes for portraiture and sculpture. He painted on canvas and in fresco, with biblical, mythological and allegorical subjects as well as portraits and nudes. The quality of the brothers' work brought commissions from courts all over Europe. Gaetano lived from 1734 to 1802.

Emanuel Leutze is best known for Washington Crossing the Delaware, from 1851. His parents brought him to the United States as a child, and his talent first showed while he sat at his father's sickbed and drew to fill the long hours. After his father died he supported himself by painting portraits at 14 for five dollars apiece. His first art instruction came in 1834 from the portrait painter John Rubens Smith in Philadelphia. He died in 1868.

Frans Pourbus the Younger was the third generation of a family of religious and portrait painters. He worked as court painter for the Archdukes in Brussels, then for the Gonzaga Duke of Mantua from 1600, and then for the French court. Most of his work was royal portraits, many of them full-length, but he also painted some altarpieces. His portraits pleased his patrons, though they are somewhat static, with no dramatic situations or landscape backgrounds. He is noted for his depiction of costume, jewellery and draperies. He died in Paris in 1622.

Paulus Constantijn la Fargue came from an artistic family in The Hague. His father worked as a notary and translator, and his siblings Isaac Lodewijk, Jacob Elias, Karel and Maria Margaretha were all painters. In 1761 he and Jacob joined the painters' society Confrerie Pictura. He was probably entirely self taught, and at first he made painted wall hangings, some commissioned by the art dealer Gerard Hoet. He is described as the most productive member of the family. He died in 1782.

Jacopo Caraglio worked as an engraver, goldsmith and medallist, and sources give his birthplace as Verona or Parma. From 1526 or earlier he worked in Rome as an engraver in collaboration with other artists, and then in Venice. In Italy he was one of the first reproductive printmakers, rendering specially made drawings or paintings, though comparison with surviving drawings shows he had some input into the creative process. He spent the rest of his life as a court goldsmith in Poland, where he died in 1565.

Hishikawa Moronobu was the son of an embroiderer in Hoda, at the far end of Edo Bay, who made work for temples and wealthy patrons. His first designs were for embroidery. In the 1660s he moved to Edo, where he studied both Tosa and Kanō painting. That gave him a grounding in decorative crafts and in academic painting, and it served him well when he turned to ukiyo-e. He is known for popularizing ukiyo-e woodblock prints and paintings in the late 17th century. He died in 1694.

The youngest of 15 children, Dankvart Dreyer came from Assens on the island of Funen and studied under Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg. Around 1840 he was part of the National Romantic landscape scene in Denmark, but his over-dramatic and excessively natural style did not fit its ideas. He was widely criticized, turned his back on the artistic establishment and passed into near oblivion. He died of typhus in 1852, at 36. Half a century later the art historian Karl Madsen restored his reputation.

Charles Leickert learned painting in The Hague from Bartholomeus van Hove, Wijnand Nuijen and Andreas Schelfhout. He specialised in winter scenes, sometimes romanticising the sky in pale blues and bright pinks, and he also painted many cityscapes. He painted almost all his works in the Netherlands, and in 1856 he became a member of the Royal Academy of Amsterdam. At 71 he moved to Mainz in Germany. He was born in Brussels and died in 1907.

A pacifist as well as an artist, Frederika Henriëtte Broeksmit founded an organization called Si vis Pacem, para Pacem. She studied at the academy in Rotterdam, at the Rijksakademie and at the National Normal School for Drawing Teachers, and she was a member of De Independents and Arti et Amicitiae. Her work was shown at the Brussels International Exhibition of 1910. In 1915 she attended the International Congress of Women at The Hague. She died in Bussum in 1945.

Anthonis Mor developed a formal style for court portraits, largely based on Titian, that influenced court painters across Europe, especially in the Iberian Peninsula, where it created a tradition that led to Velázquez. Little is known about his early life, except that he began his training under Jan van Scorel in Utrecht. His earliest known work is a portrait dated 1538, now in a collection in Stockholm. He signed most of his portraits Anthonis Mor, though he is also called Antonio Moro. He died in 1577.

Vivant Denon was sent to Paris to study law, but he preferred art and literature and soon gave up the profession. His comedy Le Bon Père won a succès d'estime, and he became a favorite of Louis XV. Napoleon appointed him the first director of the Louvre after the Egyptian campaign, and the Denon Wing is named for him. His two-volume Voyage dans la basse et la haute Egypte, from 1802, was foundational for modern Egyptology. He was made a baron by Napoleon in 1812.

William Henry Hunt's uncle, a butcher, once said of him, He was always a poor cripple, and as he was fit for nothing, they made an artist of him. Hunt had deformed legs, which may have led him to give up landscape for still life and figures. In 1806 he persuaded his father, a tin-plate worker, to let him train as an artist, and he was apprenticed to John Varley. His detailed still lifes of fruit, flowers and birds' nests earned him the nickname Bird's Nest Hunt. He died in 1864.

Joseph August Knip was the son of the decorative painter Nicolaas Frederik Knip, who was his first teacher. At nineteen he became the family breadwinner after his father went blind. In 1801 he settled in Paris, where he took commissions for topographical paintings and became drawing master to Louis Napoléon. After nine years there he went to Rome, and watercolours survive from his trips around Naples and the Sabine and Alban Hills. He returned to the Netherlands in 1813 with his wife, the painter Pauline Rifer de Courcelles. He also taught his younger sister Henriëtte Geertruida Knip.

Simon Vouet and Daniel Rabel both taught Gabriel Perelle. He specialised in classical landscapes like those of Francisque Millet, though more obviously decorative. He founded an etching workshop, where his sons Nicolas and Adam assisted him. In 1665 Louis XIV appointed him Directeur des Plans et des Cartes du Cabinet du Roi. He made several hundred engravings, from his own drawings and those of artists such as Israel Silvestre and Jacques Callot, mostly landscapes of the Paris region. He added ruins to give the views variety.

Valentine Green's father placed him in a solicitor's office at Evesham, but after two years he decided on his own to leave the law and became a pupil of a line engraver at Worcester. In London he began work as a mezzotint engraver, having taught himself the technique. He was appointed mezzotint engraver to the King in 1773. In the 1790s several of his international speculations failed, and in 1798 he was declared bankrupt. He later became keeper of the British Institution and held the post until his death in 1813.

In his day Ottavio Leoni was the most fashionable portraitist in Rome. He trained first with his father, Lodovico Leoni, and painted altarpieces for Roman churches, among them an Annunciation for Sant'Eustachio. He became a member and later president of the Accademia di San Luca. He also engraved a set of portraits of painters. His portrait of Caravaggio is the only documented portrait of the painter by another artist. He died in Rome in 1630.

Samuel Morse earned money at Yale by painting portraits of fellow students and teachers. His painting Landing of the Pilgrims caught the eye of the artist Washington Allston, who arranged a three-year stay in England for painting study. There Morse perfected his techniques under Allston, and by the end of 1811 he was admitted to the Royal Academy. After establishing his reputation as a portrait painter, he contributed in middle age to a single-wire telegraph system. He co-developed Morse code, which carries his name. He died in 1872.

Bartholomeus Spranger worked in Prague as a court artist for the emperor Rudolf II and developed a version of Northern Mannerism that stressed sensuality, with smooth, elongated figures in elegant poses. He was the third son of an Antwerp trader. He apprenticed with Jan Mandijn, then briefly with Frans Mostaert, and finally spent four years with Cornelis van Dalem. In 1565 he went to Paris, and then on to Italy. Prints spread his work widely, and Karel van Mander, who worked with him, carried his style to the Dutch Republic. He died in 1611.
